name: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
title: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
answer: Valuing illiquid tokens covers the accounting and reporting work needed when a digital asset has no reliable, active market price. It applies to tokens subject to lockups, vesting schedules, transfer restrictions, thin trading, or concentrated holdings. The work supports financial statements, fund net asset values, tax provisions, impairment testing, and transaction pricing. It also covers the difference between a token's quoted price and the price a holder could realistically obtain.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Valuing illiquid tokens covers the accounting and reporting work needed when a digital asset has no reliable, active market price. It applies to tokens subject to lockups, vesting schedules, transfer restrictions, thin trading, or concentrated holdings. The work supports financial statements, fund net asset values, tax provisions, impairment testing, and transaction pricing. It also covers the difference between a token's quoted price and the price a holder could realistically obtain.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of market data, on-chain data, and internal records. Teams pull prices and depth from exchanges, over-the-counter desks, and decentralized exchange pools, then reconcile them with token contracts, wallet balances, and vesting schedules. Spreadsheets, general ledgers, and crypto accounting systems hold the calculations, while block explorers and node providers supply transaction history. Version control and data warehouses help keep the inputs reproducible.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by defining the unit of account and the principal market, or the most advantageous market if no principal market exists. They then choose a valuation approach: market approach for observable transactions, income approach for expected cash flows, or cost approach in limited cases. Adjustments are common for lockups, market depth, bid-ask spread, volatility, and holding size. A discount for lack of marketability or a model such as a discounted cash flow or option pricing model may be used, with inputs documented and classified under the fair value hierarchy. The result is reconciled to on-chain supply and the holder's legal rights.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance, control, and restrictions. The file should show where each price came from, who approved it, and how the token contract limits transfer or sale. Risks include stale or manipulated prices, concentrated ownership, custody failures, and changing tax or regulatory treatment. Controls include segregation of duties, independent review, model validation, and a clear audit trail from source data to reported value. Disclosures should explain the valuation inputs and the uncertainty around the number.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more standardized valuation inputs and better on-chain provenance. Tokenization of funds, private credit, and real assets is creating more illiquid tokens that need consistent accounting. Regulators and standard setters are paying closer attention to fair value disclosure and custody. AI tools are likely to help with data extraction, anomaly detection, and audit trails, but human review of assumptions will remain central. The direction points to more real-time net asset value reporting and more automated reconciliation between ledgers and blockchains.
